To distinguish “acordar” (to decide) from “acordarse de” (to remember), and “despedir” (to fire, to see off) from “despedirse de” (to say goodbye).
To use “llevar / llevarse (bien, mal)” and “quedar / quedarse (con)” with their different meanings.

To use the construction “ocurrírsele algo a alguien” (se me ocurrió una idea) and involuntary “se”.
To use “irse”, “dormirse”, “morirse”, “caerse” to stress the beginning or completeness of an action.
Rosa Elena’s idea
Monday, 15 June, evening, at Ecaterina’s. In three days it will be a year since Andrés died. Ecaterina doesn’t know whether to go to Madrid. Ana and Rosa Elena have come to see her.
On Thursday it’ll be a year. I remember everything: Marta’s phone call, the two coffee cups.
Are you going to Madrid? Marta says they’re all meeting at El Mostrador at six.
I refuse to get on another plane this month. I’ve already said goodbye to him twice.
I’ve had an idea! What if we all light a lamp at the same time?
All of us? In Madrid, Bucharest and Seville at once?
Yes. And Costel in his lorry. And Grandpa Gheorghe in the village. That way nobody is left alone.
You’re like your grandmother Carmen: you always come up with things nobody else thinks of.
Then that’s agreed. Six o’clock Madrid time, which is seven here.
Seven. The time he used to switch on the bookshop lamp. It couldn’t be any other time.
And can I keep the little lamp in the living room? It’s just that it’s the one I like best.

The “rr” is rolled: o-ku-RRIR-se-le. The written accent on the “í” keeps the verb’s stress when pronouns are attached.
The diphthong “ue” appears only under stress: me a-CUER-do, but a-cor-DAR-se, nos a-cor-DA-mos.
“c” before “e” is pronounced [θ] in Spain: pa-re-THER-se. In the first person: me pa-RE-zco [pa-REθ-ko].

3. Ocurrírsele algo a alguien
Like “gustar”, the person is the indirect object and the idea is the subject:

Without “se”, “ocurrir” means “to happen”: «¿Qué ocurrió?» = What happened?

Doña Remedios went back to Seville on Monday 1 June, on the ten o’clock train. Faustino went to see her off at Atocha station in his special-occasions beret, although nobody had asked him to. Curro said afterwards that, as his grandmother got on the train, Faustino had given her a book wrapped in newspaper and told her not to open it until she reached Seville. Doña Remedios refused to wait: she opened it before the train left Madrid. It was a book of poems by Machado, with a dedication on the first page: “So you don’t forget there are poets in Castile too.”

Three days later, Faustino did something nobody expected: he bought a mobile phone. It was the first of his life. He chose it in a shop on calle Atocha, with Andrei’s help, and it took him a whole week to learn to send a message. The first one he sent, at eleven at night on 8 June, went to Seville. It said just one word, without an accent and with a spelling mistake: “Lorka”. Doña Remedios replied the next morning with another: “Machado”. From then on they wrote to each other every day.

Faustino’s messages grew longer and longer, with fewer and fewer mistakes, because doña Remedios corrected them all, one by one, with an imaginary red pen. He complained that she was worse than a schoolteacher. She replied that if he wanted to write to a bookseller, he had to learn to write like a bookseller. In mid-June, Faustino asked Andrei to teach him how to type accents on his phone. It took Andrei a whole afternoon. In the end, Faustino sent his first message without mistakes: “Machado is still better.” Doña Remedios replied with a single sign: “¿?”.

In Bucharest, June arrived with heat and lime trees in flower. On 12 June, Rosa Elena finished kindergarten. The end-of-year celebration was held in the playground, with the parents sitting on children’s chairs that were far too small for them. Each child had to recite something. The teacher had asked Rosa Elena what she wanted to recite, and she had chosen, without hesitating, a line by Machado that Ecaterina had taught her: “Traveller, there is no road, the road is made by walking.” In Spanish. In front of a hundred Romanian parents who didn’t understand a thing.

She recited it standing, very seriously, with her hands behind her back, looking at Ecaterina, who was sitting in the front row with her stick. When she finished, there was silence. Then everyone clapped, although they didn’t know what they had heard. Ecaterina didn’t clap: she sat still, her eyes wet. Later she told Ana that Andrés had recited that very line to her in 1979, by the lake in the Retiro, and that she had forgotten she had taught it to the little girl. Memory, she said, keeps things you don’t know you’ve kept.

After the celebration, the teacher came over to Ecaterina. She told her the Friday Spanish class had been a success, that the children said goodbye at the door with “hasta luego” and that one mother had complained because her son refused to say “mulțumesc” and only said “gracias”. She asked whether next year, in the preparatory class, Rosa Elena could go on teaching the class. Ecaterina told her she would have to ask Rosa Elena herself, who was very demanding about her conditions.

Rosa Elena agreed, but on conditions. She dictated them aloud in the car on the way home, and Ana had to write them on a napkin. She wanted the class to last a whole hour, not half an hour. She wanted the children to be able to bring books from home, even if they were in Romanian. And she wanted Ecaterina to come once a month to read them a story in Spanish, in her reading voice, the one she used at launches. When Ecaterina heard, she said nobody had set her such clear conditions in forty years, and she accepted them all.

That same week, Ecaterina finished the Romanian translation of her own book. It would be called “Lampa aprinsă”. It had taken her five months, twice as long as other people’s novels, because every time she translated a sentence she thought of how to improve the original, and had to stop herself from rewriting everything. The Bucharest publisher agreed to bring it out in October, with Andrei’s same cover. Ecaterina refused to change the photo, although the Romanian sales director proposed one of the Eiffel Tower, without anyone understanding why.

Andrei, for his part, received copies of the Barcelona magazine with his feature that week. Six pages, with the photo of the lamp at night taking up a whole page. He sent one to his father by express post. Señor Dan bought ten more at a kiosk in Bucharest that sold foreign newspapers, although he didn’t understand the Catalan in the captions. He handed them out to the neighbours in his block, the administrator, the local mechanic and his former colleagues at the bridge company. He told them all the same thing: “The photos are my son’s. The text doesn’t matter.”

There were three days to go until 18 June. Ecaterina had spent the whole week not knowing what to do. Marta had told her that in Madrid they were all going to meet at El Mostrador, at six in the evening, to remember her grandfather. Pilar would come from Seville. But Ecaterina refused to get on another plane that month. She had been to Madrid in April and in May, and said her body of over eighty no longer got on well with airports. Besides, she told Ana, she had already said goodbye to him twice. A third time seemed too much.

It was Rosa Elena who found the solution, as she nearly always did. She was on the living-room floor, drawing, while her mother and Ecaterina talked. Suddenly she looked up and said she had had an idea: what if they all lit a lamp at the same time, each wherever they were? In Madrid, in Bucharest, in Seville. Costel in his lorry. Grandpa Gheorghe in the village. That way nobody would be left alone. Ecaterina looked at her for a moment and told her she took after her grandmother Carmen, because she always came up with things nobody else thought of.

They agreed on the time in five minutes: six in Madrid, which was seven in Bucharest. Ecaterina said it couldn’t be any other time, because at seven o’clock sharp Andrés used to switch on the bookshop lamp, every evening, for seventeen years. Ana wrote the message in the club’s group chat, with the exact words Rosa Elena dictated. At the end, the little girl added one condition: if anyone forgot, it didn’t matter, because she would stay awake and switch it on for them. Ana reminded her that seven o’clock wasn’t bedtime yet. Rosa Elena said: just in case.

The message travelled further than anyone expected. Marta forwarded it to Pilar, Lola, Faustino, Begoña and Inés. Faustino, with his new phone, forwarded it to doña Remedios, without accents and with two mistakes. Costel sent it to Zoltán, who sent it to all the Hungarian lorry drivers in his group. Lola printed it and stuck it in the window of El Mostrador, below the plaque, for the neighbours to read. Within two days, a six-year-old girl’s message had reached people who had never known Andrés.

The day before, Ecaterina called Marta. She asked whether they were ready in Madrid. Marta told her Lola had cleaned the lamp at the back with a damp cloth, bulb by bulb, and Faustino had bought a table lamp to take to the café, just in case there wasn’t enough light. Pilar had arrived from Seville that very afternoon, with a bunch of orange blossom. And Begoña, who never went to anything, had asked what time it was exactly. Ecaterina asked whether Begoña was going to come. Marta said she didn’t know; with Begoña you never knew anything until the last minute.

Thursday 18 June dawned cloudy in Bucharest. Ecaterina got up at six, as always, and made a single cup of coffee. She remembered the morning a year earlier, the two cups, Marta’s call. But she didn’t cry. She sat in her armchair with the cup in her hands and looked at the little lamp in the living room, the one Rosa Elena had asked to keep one day. She thought a year was very little time to miss someone, and a very long time for someone who had waited forty.

At midday Ana called to ask whether she wanted them to have lunch together. Ecaterina said no, she preferred to spend the day alone until the evening. She ate little, had a nap and, when she woke up, put on the blue dress she had worn at the Madrid launch. Then she took Andrés’s copy of Rayuela off the shelf, with the two letters inside, and put it on the living-room table, beside the little lamp. She didn’t open it. She just wanted it to be there, close to the light.

In the evening, at half past six, Ecaterina’s living room began to fill up. Ana, Mihai and Rosa Elena arrived. Mrs Florica arrived with her husband, who for the first time was leaving the house for something other than a Rapid match. Señor Dan and his wife arrived. Costel couldn’t come: he was in a car park near Linz, in Austria, with a load of timber. But he had promised to join by video call. At five to seven, Ana put her phone on the table, propped against a vase, and connected with Madrid.

On the screen El Mostrador appeared, with the evening light coming in through the window. Everyone was there: Marta, Andrei, Lola, Pilar with Manuel, Carmen and Juan, the twins from Lavapiés and, at the table at the back, Faustino, with his new phone in his hand and doña Remedios on its screen, connected from her bookshop in Triana. Lola had removed all the chairs at the back so the lamp could be seen clearly. Nobody spoke. You could hear the coffee machine, the noise of calle de las Huertas and, now and then, Faustino asking Andrei which button to press.

At seven o’clock sharp Bucharest time, six in Madrid, Rosa Elena got up, went to the little lamp in the living room and switched it on. On the screen, at the same moment, Lola switched on the one at the back of El Mostrador, and Marta, beside her, switched on the second one too, in the window. On Faustino’s phone, doña Remedios lit an old lamp in her bookshop, a green glass one. And on another screen, Mihai’s phone, Costel appeared in his lorry cab, in Austria, switching on the ceiling light. Behind him, in the car park, other lights could be seen.

Costel explained quietly what was happening. Zoltán had forwarded the message to his group of drivers, and that evening, in car parks in Hungary, Austria, Slovakia and Germany, dozens of lorry drivers who didn’t know who Andrés was had switched on their cab lights at the same time. In the Linz car park there were six lorries with their lights on. One of the drivers, a very large Pole, had come over to Costel’s cab to ask who they were switching them on for. Costel had explained. The Pole had taken off his cap.

In the village, Grandpa Gheorghe had no video calls, but Mihai had called him on the landline a few minutes earlier. Grandpa had told him not to worry, he knew already, the neighbour had read him the message. At seven, he had lit an old oil lamp, the one they used in the village before electricity arrived, and put it in the window facing the road, under the walnut tree. Then he had called Mihai to say it was done. “Por fin,” he had said in Spanish. And then: “Salud.”

For five minutes nobody said anything, in Bucharest, Madrid, Seville or the car park in Linz. The lamps were lit. The screens trembled a little. Ecaterina looked at the little lamp in the living room and, now and then, at the one at the back of El Mostrador on the screen, as if they were the same. She thought she had never been as close to Andrés as at that moment, two thousand kilometres from his grave. She also thought he would have laughed at all this, and then said: “Pues muy bien.”

It was Faustino who broke the silence, without meaning to. Trying to turn on the speaker so doña Remedios could hear better, he pressed the wrong button and El Mostrador filled with a reggaeton song at full volume that Andrei had downloaded to test the phone. Faustino went as red as a tomato and couldn’t switch it off. Doña Remedios, in Seville, burst out laughing. So did Lola. Then Marta, Pilar, Carmen, and finally the whole café. In Bucharest, Rosa Elena started dancing. Ecaterina said Andrés would have hated the song and adored the moment.

Andrei sent Ecaterina, that same night, a photo he had taken at one minute past six Madrid time, while everyone was silent. It showed El Mostrador from the street, through the window: the three lamps lit, the bronze plaque shining and, inside, with her back to the camera, a woman with very short grey hair, standing by the door, not sitting down. It was Begoña. She had arrived at two minutes to six, without warning, and left at ten past six, without saying goodbye to anyone. Andrei had only seen her through his lens.

Later, when they had all said goodbye on the video call, Pilar called Ecaterina on the phone, just the two of them. She told her that during the five minutes of silence she had been looking at the first copy of the book, the “At last, delivered” one, under the lamp, with the two bookmarks peeping out from between the pages: doña Remedios’s from 1958 and Ecaterina’s from 1983. She said that, looking at them, it had occurred to her that her father had drawn the same lamp all his life, and that at last someone had really lit it.

That night, Rosa Elena refused to go to bed until Ecaterina promised her something. Ecaterina asked what. The little girl said she wanted to keep the little lamp in the living room, but not now, when she was grown up, so she could switch it on at seven every evening, like Señor Andrés. Ecaterina promised. Then Rosa Elena fell asleep on the sofa, with her head on her father’s knees. Ecaterina left the lamp on all night. For the first time in a year, she went to bed without remembering the two coffee cups.

In the days that followed, messages from strangers began to arrive. A Hungarian lorry driver sent Costel a photo of his lit cab with a sentence in Spanish learnt from a translation app: “For the bookseller gentleman I didn’t know.” A neighbour on calle de las Huertas left an old table lamp at El Mostrador, with a note: “So there are three.” Lola put it in the window, next to the second one. And doña Remedios wrote to Faustino, with every accent in its place: “I thought of you at one minute past six.” It took Faustino two days to reply, because he didn’t know how.

At the end of June, Faustino did something else nobody expected: he closed his stall for a whole week, for the first time in sixty years, and went to Seville by train. He told Andrei he was going to see an old bookshop in Triana, for professional reasons. Andrei asked whether he needed him to take any photos of the bookshop. Faustino replied no, this time he would take the photos himself, with his new phone. The first ones he sent to the group, from Triana, were all blurred. The only one that wasn’t showed doña Remedios laughing under an orange tree.

Marta saw the photo in Madrid and opened her novel notebook. The novel was called, for now, “The Bookseller of Triana”, and already had forty pages. Andrei asked whether she knew yet how it would end. Marta said no, the two of them were writing it for her, live, from Seville, and she was just taking notes. Andrei asked whether that wasn’t a bit like cheating. Marta replied that her grandfather had taught her that the best stories aren’t invented: they are listened to, and then you remember them.

On 30 June, the last Thursday of the month, Costel and Señor Dan had their last study session before the C1 exam, which was on 11 July. They held it in the lorry cab, as always, parked outside Señor Dan’s block. Ecaterina joined by video call from her armchair. She gave them an exercise on verbs that change meaning with “se”. Costel got “acordar” and “acordarse” wrong. Señor Dan, “despedir” and “despedirse”. Ecaterina told them not to worry, even Andrés got those verbs wrong when he was nervous.

Costel asked her when Andrés used to get nervous. Ecaterina thought for a moment. Then she said only once, as far as she could remember. It was in 1985, on the Cuesta de Moyano, the day of Faustino’s photo, when he asked her to marry him for the second time. He said “te acuerdo” instead of “te quiero”, from nerves, and she burst out laughing, and so did he, and that was why they were both laughing in the photo. Costel and Señor Dan sat silent in the cab. Then Costel said he would never again get “acordarse” wrong. And he never did.
